### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.4.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)   # 3.0.4
print(pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h"))
```

### Issue Description

On **pandas 3.0.4 + Python 3.14**, `pd.date_range(..., freq="h")` raises an `OverflowError` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. The `freq` argument is silently reinterpreted as an astronomically large `Hours` offset (e.g. `<281467879224592 * Hours>`) instead of `<1 * Hours>`.

The same call works correctly on **pandas 3.0.3 + Python 3.14**.

### Full traceback

```
pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.pyx:2014: OverflowError

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

start = Timestamp('2026-04-17 00:00:00'), end = None, periods = 24
freq = <281467879224592 * Hours>, unit = 'us'

    def generate_regular_range(...):
        ...
        try:
            td = td.as_unit(unit, round_ok=False)
        except ValueError as err:
            raise ValueError(
                f"freq={freq} is incompatible with unit={unit}. "
                "Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead."
            ) from err

pandas/core/arrays/_ranges.py:74: ValueError:
  freq=<281467879224592 * Hours> is incompatible with unit=us.
  Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead.
```

Also observed as:

```
pandas.errors.OutOfBoundsTimedelta:
  Cannot cast 11727828301024 days 16:00:00 to unit='us' without overflow.
```

### Expected Behavior

`pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h")` should return a `DatetimeIndex` of 24 hourly timestamps, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

### Installed Versions

- pandas: **3.0.4** (regression; **3.0.3** works)
- Python: **3.14.6**
- Platform: Linux (Docker, `linux/amd64`)

Note: `freq="h"` (lowercase) is the recommended alias since pandas 2.2 (replacing the deprecated `"H"`), so this is not a deprecated-alias issue.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hi! I would like to propose that scikit-learn should start publishing Pyodide/WASM wheels, i.e., with the [pyemscripten](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/development/abi.html) platform tag as per the accepted and implemented [PEP 783](https://peps.python.org/pep-0783/), to PyPI, for both ABIs that we currently support:
- the 2025 ABI (corresponding to [Pyodide 0.29.4](https://pyodide.org/en/0.29.4/), built with CPython 3.13 and Emscripten 4.0.9); and
- the 2026 ABI (corresponding to the [new Pyodide 314.0.0 release](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/), read our [blog post](https://blog.pyodide.org/posts/314-release/) – built with CPython 3.14 and Emscripten 5.0.3).

This follows on from the RFC for Pyodide being regarded as a _somewhat_ officially supported platform posted at https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/23727, and resolved as of June 2025 (just about a year ago!).

The rationale to build this case is also Pyodide's ever-growing maturity and stability as a platform, highlighted by the PEP's [acceptance](https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-783-emscripten-packaging/86862/104), [official Tier III CPython 3.14 support as per the active PEP 776](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html); and our various cross-compilation infrastructure, packaging, and interoperability improvements over the years; besides scikit-learn's usage of Pyodide for its JupyterLite-powered interactive documentation offerings and well-established testing as part of the CI test suite.

### Describe your proposed solution

The scikit-learn wheels are built with [cibuildwheel](https://cibuildwheel.pypa.io/) everywhere across the board. [cibuildwheel v4.1.0](https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/releases/tag/v4.1.0), released on 12th June, 2026, i.e., yesterday at the time of writing, is capable of building and publishing Pyodide wheels with `CIBW_PLATFORM: pyodide` environment variable or the `--platform pyodide` command-line flag-argument pair for both the 2025 and 2026 ABIs, with all batteries included. A comprehensive set of documentation for pyodide-build is available at https://pyodide-build.readthedocs.io, thanks to @ryanking13. A release blog post for cibuildwheel v4 is also available at https://iscinumpy.dev/post/cibuildwheel-4-0-0/.

As a result, this should be a simple switch (famous last words?). It would only require meddling with the workflow files to integrate uploading such built wheels to PyPI, while ensuring that the test suite is green for both ABIs.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The best alternative is the status quo itself, in that scikit-learn keeps running its test suite for Pyodide without publishing wheels, and we retain its recipe at https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes. However, such a scenario would not be ideal for us, as we plan to scale down the scope of that repository as we work towards supporting the adoption of this PEP across the ecosystem: https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-build/issues/290, https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes/issues/599, https://pyodide.github.io/are-we-pep783-yet. In that sense, successful adoption of the PEP essentially allows us to offload maintenance of the packages' WASM build pipelines to willing package maintainers. This enables us to spend more time on other maintenance needs and on feature development for Pyodide's foreign function interface, integration with downstream codebases for kernel federation capabilities such as JupyterLite and its Pyodide kernel (which I maintain), as well as on bespoke packaging infrastructure and performance improvements.

### Additional context

- A frequently asked question that follows naturally from my proposal, which I estimate will come up early and should be discussed, is whether scikit-learn's main, non-optional dependencies provide such support, and whether they would adopt PEP 783. Here are some points to serve some extra context, since I am cognisant of the fact that going from a well-tested, de facto supported platform to an officially supported-via-distributed-binaries platform is a sizeable leap:
  - NumPy: is an officially listed Tier III platform as per [NEP 57 – NumPy platform support](https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0057-numpy-platform-support.html#tier-3), which means that it currently does not publish pyemscripten wheels to PyPI. This NEP was proposed and sprang into action during a time when PEP 783 was under discussion, and, might I say, in the ambit of being accepted, but had not been accepted yet. There is a chance that this situation might change and we might be elevated into Tier II at some point, subject to the NumPy steering council deeming it acceptable to happen. However, I have yet to ask about this in the NumPy issue tracker. The Pyodide cross-build environments currently provide a Frankenstein version of WASM-built NumPy, termed a cross-built package, which is non-cross-compiled but includes WASM-specific headers. This has been the case for many years now, and scikit-learn will automatically pull in this NumPy build from the `pyodide xbuildenv` when building its WASM distributions. We support retrieving wheels for packages from both a local locked index that ships with the xbuildenv and PyPI simultaneously, which means that NumPy will be brought in from either place when installing scikit-learn, and thus it is not a requirement for scikit-learn to need to wait for NumPy to adopt PEP 783 as such before it itself does so – besides the obvious reason of community stewardship in the Scientific Python ecosystem, of course.
  - SciPy: is well-supported in Pyodide. @lesteve has been a maintainer of and has contributed various improvements to the SciPy recipe and OpenBLAS integration for previous releases (ref: [Loïc's talk from EuroSciPy 2023](https://youtube.com/watch?v=n8-r_zjpupk)) along with Pyodide maintainers. I have picked up maintenance from time to time for more recent releases of SciPy over the last two years, during and post my work as part of the [CZI 2022 Scientific Python grant](https://blog.scientific-python.org/scientific-python/2022-czi-grant/). SciPy suffers from the lack of (integration of) a proper Fortran-to-WASM compiler such as LLVM-Flang. Therefore, it requires various patches to build OpenBLAS and various extension modules, which are difficult to upstream, and thereby it has existed as a recipe in the pyodide-recipes repository. However, with all the Fortran code gone in SciPy-dev (xref https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/18566) and a Fortran-compiler-free build also available soon, and a vastly reduced number of skips and crashes for the SciPy test suite in Pyodide (see my most recent updates in https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes/pull/586 – pretty promising!), there is a chance that SciPy can gain Pyodide interoperability that is as close as possible to what is observed within a more conventional platform-architecture combination.
  - narwhals: is supported (and tested) in Pyodide and is a pure Python dependency. No change is needed.
  - joblib and threadpoolctl both have Emscripten/Pyodide support. This has been contributed and maintained over the years, courtesy of @lesteve and a number of contributors.

- I posted this discussion as a thread in the scikit-learn Discord server first, at the following link: https://discord.com/channels/731163543038197871/1046822941586898974/1514624149107114046, where it was suggested that I should open this as an issue here.

- I believe there were some conversations about older versions of Pyodide being used in the WASM notebooks back when a subset of the scikit-learn crowd (not tagging everyone here; y'all will come across this proposal at some point anyway! 😄) and I were present at the [Scientific Python Developer Summit in Copenhagen in November 2025](https://scientific-python.org/summits/developer/2025-nov/). We discussed a few Pyodide-related topics, but I did not follow the WASM notebooks topic too closely. I believe it would be helpful to discuss any other items that need to be implemented as part of this proposal, so we can spend time on them and cover any gaps in Pyodide support. The Pyodide team would be willing to contribute support towards any missing pieces of the picture. If this proposal is accepted, I would be happy to start out on a list of tasks towards implementing it across CI, docs, etc., and contribute to scikit-learn in the process!

cc: @hoodmane and @ryanking13 as co-maintainers of Pyodide, for visibility, and in case they would like to add anything I missed.

Thank you for your time!

## BUG: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from pandas.plotting._matplotlib.style import get_standard_colors

print(f"matplotlib: {matplotlib.__version__}")  # 3.11.0
print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")              # 3.0.3

# Returns hex strings with mpl 3.10.x, RGB tuples with mpl 3.11.0
colors = get_standard_colors(num_colors=3)
print(colors)
# mpl 3.10.9: ['#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c']
# mpl 3.11.0: [(0.122..., 0.467..., 0.706...), (1.0, 0.498..., 0.055...), (0.173..., 0.627..., 0.173...)]

# Same issue with Line2D.get_color()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3])
print(repr(line.get_color()))
# mpl 3.10.9: '#1f77b4'
# mpl 3.11.0: (0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)
plt.close()

# The colors are numerically identical:
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
print(to_hex((0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)))
# '#1f77b4'
```

### Issue Description

With matplotlib 3.11.0 (released 2026-06-12), the default property cycle now returns colors as RGB tuples rather than hex strings. This causes 5 pandas plotting tests to fail:

- `tests/plotting/test_boxplot_method.py::TestDataFramePlots::test_colors_in_theme[default-expected1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_series.py::TestSeriesPlots::test_pie_series_autopct_and_fontsize`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[1-expected_name0]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[3-expected_name1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[12-expected_name2]`

The upstream matplotlib change is https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/29469 ("Separate property cycle handling from _process_plot_var_args"), merged in commit [`ec65514`](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/commit/ec655143528f8e8dbc7897cc3c1e59865672c7ef) and released as part of [matplotlib 3.11.0](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/releases/tag/v3.11.0). This refactored the internal property cycle machinery into a dedicated class. As a side effect, the default `axes.prop_cycle` rcParam now stores colors as `(R, G, B)` float tuples rather than hex strings.

The relevant matplotlib milestone: https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/milestone/96

All affected APIs are public:
- `mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle']` — iterating over the cycler now yields `{'color': (R, G, B)}` dicts instead of `{'color': '#rrggbb'}` dicts
- `Line2D.get_color()` — returns whatever format was stored in the cycle, now a tuple instead of a string

The behavior change is observable through these public APIs, though matplotlib has never formally guaranteed a specific color *format* (both hex strings and RGB tuples are valid matplotlib color specifications). The pandas tests assert a specific format (hex strings) rather than comparing semantically.

### Expected Behavior

Tests should pass with matplotlib 3.11.0. The test assertions should either:

1. Normalize colors before comparison (e.g., using `matplotlib.colors.to_hex()` or `matplotlib.colors.same_color()`), or
2. Compare in a format-agnostic way that handles both hex strings and RGB tuples.

Additionally, if `get_standard_colors()` has a documented contract about its return format, it may be worth normalizing the output within that function itself so downstream consumers aren't affected by matplotlib's internal representation changes.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

To ensure thread-safety, it's useful to have test infrastructure that will provide:

* A way to identify thread-safety issues in code that has previously mostly been run in process pools. Free-threading's lack of GIL makes thread safety issues more likely than in the past.
* A way to prevent _future changes_ to the code introducing new thread-safety problems.
* 🆕 A way to identify which parts of a data structure are intended to be thread-safe, and which are not.

A good starting point here is focusing on operations that are _already_ parallel, where users might reasonably expect to be able to turn threading on as a `joblib` backend and have it Just Work. These operations also work in a very particular way: create some tasks, run them in a worker pool, get back the results of the tasks.

What can go wrong in this particular idiom? Switching from a process pool to a thread pool introduces thread-safety issues with the _inputs_ to a `Parallel()` operation: whereas mutating in a process is fine, mutating in a thread can affect other threads, or future interactions with the object in the main thread.

This suggests a starting point for a invariant to be using in testing: **the inputs to a `Parallel()` operation that can correctly run with both process and thread pools should not change when the function is run.**

🆕 This invariant will not be true for objects that are _designed_ to be mutated safely, so there needs to be a way to opt out of the check.

### Describe your proposed solution

When `pytest` is run (no extra flags! 🆕) and `Parallel()`'s backend a thread pool

* Arguments passed to functions called in parallel are tracked to see if they changed as part of execution.
* "Change" is calculated heuristically, with a hash.
* If hashes change, raise an AssertionError.

🆕 There will be a mechanism to opt-out parameters, or parameter's attributes, from the hashing. In particular, they can be optionally be marked as one of:

* `thread-safe`: indicating these attributes are designed to be safely mutated from multiple threads. This should include a short explanation or pointer to explanation.
* `buggy-thread-unsafe`: indicating this is not thread-safe but is still being accessed from multiple threads. This should include a reference to a GitHub issue explaining the problem.

In addition to opt-in out of the hashing test, these will therefore also serve as documentation of thread-safety or lack thereof. They can also suggest utility classes to formalize certain idioms that repeat, e.g. one can imagine a Rust-style lock that _wraps_ an object, rather than having lock and lock-protected-object being two different parameters. Such classes would then also be automatically opted-out.

When pytest is first run with the hashing, it will fail in three ways; initial tests suggest perhaps 20 locations are affected:

* **Known thread-unsafe code:** For example, BinaryTree. This can be annotated with `ThreadSync`, with pointer to an existing issue.
* **Thread-safe code:** E.g. a result objects that is intended to used with a paired lock, an idiom used in at least one place. In this case, this can be annotated and perhaps an issue filed about formalizing the idiom into a reusable class.
* **Unknown status:** Depending how complex it is to investigate, and the investigation's conclusion, either `thread-safe` or `buggy-thread-unsafe` with issue filed to investigate it further and determine the final status.

At the end of this relatively quick process the tests should pass across the board, some new issues should be filed for follow up, and a new passing CI job can be added.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Thread sanitizers can catch some of these issues, and they should be used to validate scikit-learn thread safety over the long term. However, they are not something a developer can easily run locally: they require recompiling CPython and all relevant extensions (though there is a Docker image, but still). Whereas this approach is just a normal Python build running normal Python tests.

### Additional context

Based on https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34057, but with more details and addressing some concerns in the discussion there.

#34071 would be needed to have this run broadly.

Differences from PR are marked with 🆕, and include:

* Added use case of identifying which parts of data structure are designed to be mutable from multiple threads.
* Added notions of marking known-thread-safe code and known-buggy code.
* Removed notion of `pytest` flag, just do the test automatically.
* Removed notion of switching thread pools on automatically.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In most array API estimator methods that happen after `.fit()`, if an incompatible input is passed to the method, it throws an informative error message, usually coming from `check_same_namespace` - for example:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
Ridge(solver="svd").fit(Xd, y).predict(X)
```
```
ValueError: Inputs passed to Ridge.predict() must use the same namespace and the same device as those passed to fit(). Array namespaces used during fit (dpnp) and predict (sklearn.externals.array_api_compat.numpy) differ. You can move the estimator to the same namespace and device as X with: 'from sklearn.utils._array_api import move_estimator_to; xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(X); estimator = move_estimator_to(estimator, xp, device)'
```

The error type in this case is `ValueError`.

But PCA's methods like inverse_transform do not use that utility function, erroring out with a less informative message instead, and with the error type being `TypeError`:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/bb9df11710fc918df3110565b5145b8247c0ab47/sklearn/decomposition/_base.py#L193

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python

We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.

```python
import time
import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql
from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect

with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table
    end = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"Took {end - start} seconds")
```

The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. The default depth is `"all"`, which enumerates objects down to the columns. Adding `depth="tables"` speeds things up dramatically for us—from 53 seconds without `depth="tables"` down to 3 seconds with.

The docstring in `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` says it calculates distances up to:

import pandas as pd

pi = pd.period_range("2000Q1", periods=12, freq="Q-FEB")

### Issue Description

Partial-string slicing on a `PeriodIndex` whose frequency is anchored to a month that
does not line up with calendar quarters resolves the string bounds one period too early,
so the slice is shifted and includes an extra label at the start.

It is not specific to quarterly frequencies — anchored annual frequencies are affected
too:

```python
for anchor in ["Q-DEC", "Q-JAN", "Q-FEB", "Q-MAR", "Q-APR", "Q-NOV"]:
    ser = pd.Series(range(12), index=pd.period_range("2000Q1", periods=12, freq=anchor))
    print(anchor, list(ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"].index))

# Q-DEC ['2001Q1']                # OK
# Q-JAN ['2000Q4', '2001Q1']      # wrong
# Q-FEB ['2000Q4', '2001Q1']      # wrong
# Q-MAR ['2001Q1']                # OK
# Q-APR ['2000Q4', '2001Q1']      # wrong
# Q-NOV ['2000Q4', '2001Q1']      # wrong

for anchor in ["Y-DEC", "Y-JUN", "Y-MAR"]:
    ser = pd.Series(range(8), index=pd.period_range("2000", periods=8, freq=anchor))
    print(anchor, list(ser.loc["2002":"2002"].index))

# Y-DEC ['2002']                  # OK
# Y-JUN ['2002', '2003']          # wrong
# Y-MAR ['2002', '2003']          # wrong
```

`Q-DEC` and `Q-MAR` are correct because their quarters coincide with calendar quarters.

The cause is in `PeriodIndex._parsed_string_to_bounds`
(`pandas/core/indexes/period.py`). The string is first parsed *with* the index frequency,
which correctly applies the anchor, but the result is then re-bucketed into a **calendar**
period before being converted back, which discards the anchor:

```python
def _parsed_string_to_bounds(self, reso: Resolution, parsed: datetime):
    freq = OFFSET_TO_PERIOD_FREQSTR.get(reso.attr_abbrev, reso.attr_abbrev)
    iv = Period(parsed, freq=freq)   # <- freq is "Q"/"Y", anchor lost here
    return (iv.asfreq(self.freq, how="start"), iv.asfreq(self.freq, how="end"))
```

Traced for `"2001Q1"` on a `Q-FEB` index:

```
parse_datetime_string_with_reso("2001Q1", "Q-FEB")  ->  2000-03-01, reso="quarter"
Period(2000-03-01, freq="Q")                        ->  2000Q1      # calendar, anchor lost
.asfreq("Q-FEB", how="start"/"end")                 ->  2000Q4 .. 2001Q1
```

so the bounds span two labels instead of resolving to `Period("2001Q1", freq="Q-FEB")`.

This also reaches `DataFrame.truncate`/`Series.truncate`, which delegate to `.loc`.

### Expected Behavior

The string bound should resolve to the same period the equivalent `Period` object does, so
that `ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]` returns exactly the `2001Q1` row for every anchor:

```python
ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]
# 2001Q1    4
# Freq: Q-FEB, dtype: int64
```

i.e. the bounds should be derived using the index's own frequency
(`Period("2001Q1", freq=self.freq)`) rather than by re-bucketing the parsed datetime into a
calendar period.

### Problem Description

### Background
While investigating a memory corruption issue yesterday (reported in #65664  and patched in PR #65675 ), I found a structural vulnerability in how the computation engine interacts with Pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write (CoW) architecture. 

Specifically, `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` was bypassing CoW protections. The `eval` engine reached into the `BlockManager`, extracted the raw data arrays, evaluated them, and handed them back. Because the data took a detour through the external computation engine, the CoW reference tracking metadata was stripped. The DataFrame assumed the returned array was unshared memory, leading to silent memory corruption when the alias was later modified.

### The Architectural Question
My patch forces an explicit `.copy()` before assignment if `inplace=True` inside `pandas.core.computation.eval`. However, this raises a much larger architectural question: **Are there other C-engine, Cython, or NumExpr-routed methods that are secretly leaking CoW tracking data when `inplace=True` is invoked?**

### Proposed Audit Targets
We know that standard `__setitem__` handles CoW perfectly. But any method that extracts raw arrays, computes externally, and attempts to write back `inplace` is at risk. I propose a systematic audit of the following `inplace=True` methods to ensure they aren't making the same tracking error:

1. **`DataFrame.query(inplace=True)`:** Since this relies on the exact same underlying `pandas.core.computation` engines (`numexpr` / `python`) as `eval`, it is the most likely candidate for a parallel vulnerability.
2. **`DataFrame.where()` & `DataFrame.mask()`:** When backed by external engines or fast-path Cython blocks.
3. **`DataFrame.fillna()` & `DataFrame.replace()`:** Specifically when operating on mixed dtypes that might force a block consolidation or split during the inplace write.
4. **`DataFrame.clip()`**

### Action Items
Rather than playing whack-a-mole with memory bugs, I suggest we:
1. Identify all `inplace=True` paths that route through `numexpr` or bypass the standard `NDFrame.__setitem__` API.
2. Implement a standardized CoW "alias corruption" test suite specifically targeting these external engine routes.
3. Determine if we need a centralized validation wrapper that explicitly checks reference counts when C-engines return data for inplace assignment.

I am happy to lead the audit on `.query()` and `.where()` to start, but wanted to bring this to the core team's attention to see if there is already a broader strategy for validating `inplace` safety under CoW. Thoughts?

### Feature Description

I propose implementing a two-phase solution to secure the CoW perimeter:

**1. A Centralized Testing Utility:**
Introduce a new test utility in `pandas/tests/copy_view/` specifically designed to test external-engine mutations. 
Pseudocode:
```python

    """
    Ensures that an inplace operation does not corrupt aliases 
    if it routes through an external engine.
    """
    df_copy = df.copy()
    alias = df["column_name"]
    
    # Perform inplace operation that might strip CoW tracking
    operation_func(df) 
    
    # Mutate the alias
    alias.iloc[0] = modified_value
    
    # If the original dataframe was mutated, the CoW perimeter failed.
    assert_frame_equal(df, df_copy)

2. A C-Engine Return Wrapper:
If the audit finds multiple leaks in .query(), .where(), etc., rather than patching them individually, we should implement a validation layer inside BlockManager.setitem_inplace (or the equivalent API) that explicitly asserts: if pd.options.mode.copy_on_write: assert result.refs is safe before mapping the C-engine memory back to the dataframe.



### **Alternative Solutions**
**Alternative 1: The "Whack-a-Mole" Approach (Status Quo)**
We do nothing structurally, and wait for users to report data corruption bugs one by one as they upgrade to Pandas 3.0. This risks user trust in the new CoW architecture.

**Alternative 2: Do nothing and wait for PDEP-8**
Since `inplace=True` is broadly slated for deprecation and removal in Pandas 4.0 (PDEP-8), we could argue that investing in `inplace` infrastructure isn't worth the time. *However*, because users will be relying on Pandas 3.x during the CoW transition period, allowing silent data corruption to exist during this window is highly dangerous. We need to secure the perimeter until `inplace` is officially removed.

### Issue Description

There are three python api call patterns that ujson objToJson doesn't reliably check the result code for:
 - Converting unicode to utf8. (for example "\ud800" can fail)
 - Converting very large integers to string
 - Calling Various dunder methods that usually behave predicably.

I came into this via some fuzz testing I was doing, which found this:

```
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
```

But then a review of the `objToJSON` with the help of codex came up with the following inputs that cause ujson to segfault:
 - [ ] decimal.Decimal subclasses with a `__format__` method that returns a lone surrogate [#66357]
 - [ ] `datetime.time` subclasses whose `isoformat()` return a non-string, or lone surrogate value [#66357]
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that raise
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that return a lone surrogate value.
 - [ ] Set() subclasses whose `__iter__` raises
 - [ ] encoding int values whose string representation > `sys.get_int_max_str_digits()` digits long [#66357]
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are lone surrogate values
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are `int` values that are too long

Currently, the `n_bins` parameter in [`sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve.html) defaults to 5. Users must manually tune this parameter to balance the trade-off between bias (too few bins) and variance (too many bins).

Example: for a dataset of size $n = 100,000$, the optimal number of bins is on the order of 100, far exceeding the default 5. Using the default 5 creates a calibration curve that's overly crude.

### Describe your proposed solution
Specifically, research in the paper ["Optimal Recalibration via Uniform-Mass Binning"](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3666122.3669166) provides a theoretical proof that the optimal number of bins ($B$) for recalibration via uniform-mass binning scales with the cubic root of the number of samples ($n$). (Conflict of interest: I'm an author of the paper)

The proposed implementation would be:
```python
if n_bins == 'auto':
    n_bins = int(len(y_true) ** (1/3))
```

Benefits include:
* **Ease of Use**: Tuning free. This is also the practice for many other sklearn implementation of algorithms, e.g., 
  * `max_features` of `RandomForestClassifier` defaults to `sqrt`, which uses $\sqrt{n\\_features}$ for classifiers.
  * `gamma` of `SVC` has options `'scale'` and `'auto'`.
* **Statistical Robustness**: defaulting to a theoretically optimal value improves the reliability of calibration metrics and plots across a wider range of $n$.

### Additional context

Here's a rough description of why $\sqrt{n}$ is the optimal bin number (under some quite general assumptions):
- **Notations**: Let $Z$ be the random variable of the predicted probability to be calibrated, and $h^\star$ be the optimal calibration function $h^\star(z) := \text{E}[Y|Z=z]$. 
- **Bound of bias**: First, each bins has about $n/B$ samples, which contributes to $B/n$ factor in the calibration risk bound due to Hoeffding's inequality.
- **Bound of variance**: Then, we note the sharpness risk $\text{E}[\text{Var}(h^\star(Z)) | h(Z))]$ is the average conditional variance of $h^\star(Z)$ in each bin. Since the variance is smaller than the squared range, and the range of $h^\star(Z)$ within each bin is bounded by $O(1/B)$, we have the average conditional variance is bounded by O(1/B^2).
- **Bound of MSE**: Lastly, minimizing the sum of the two bounds $O(1/B^2 + B/n)$ yields $B \asymp n^{1/3}$.

This issue is a tracker for the task of adding chunking to the computation in `ledoit_wolf_shrinkage` (`sklearn/covariance/_shrunk_covariance.py`).

For the CPU implementation chunking is already supported. For the array API path we currently perform no chunking. Bigger chunks are better for GPU devices (in terms of execution time), but they require more memory.

After investigating and benchmarking a bit, I am not sure what we should do. For "tall and skinny" datasets blocking doesn't matter. For wide datasets it limits how much additional memory is used for temporaries. With `n_features=20_000` you'd use something like 1.6GB of extra memory without blocking. However, the speedup (MPS over numpy) when using blocking is much smaller than if the MPS implementation runs without blocking. It can be  5x - 10x without blocking and only something like 2x faster if you use `block_size=1000` for MPS as well.

Numpy is also faster if you increase the block size. For example, `block_size=2000` seems to speed things up by roughly a factor two and still only uses a small amount of memory.

So I think we could increase the block size, even for Numpy. But I am not sure how we should decide the trade-off between speed up and memory. We could use a block size like 3000 for all namespaces/devices to get most of the speed up and avoid catastrophic "out of memory" exceptions. The user could then tune the block size if they knew that they have enough memory? But it feels like I just made up 3000, it could equally be 4000 or 2000 - I couldn't argue which of these is more correct/better.

### Issue Description

`Series` construction correctly infers `object` for an integer that no NumPy/nullable integer
dtype can hold:

```python
>>> pd.Series([2**64]).dtype
dtype('O')
```

but `convert_dtypes` then tries to force that column to `Int64` regardless, and overflows:

```
  File "pandas/core/internals/blocks.py", line 582, in convert_dtypes
    rbs.append(b.astype(dtype=dtype, squeeze=b.ndim != 1))
  File "pandas/core/dtypes/astype.py", line 82, in _astype_nansafe
    return dtype.construct_array_type()._from_sequence(arr, dtype=dtype, copy=copy)
  File "pandas/core/arrays/numeric.py", line 248, in _coerce_to_data_and_mask
    values = dtype_cls._safe_cast(values, dtype, copy=False)
  File "pandas/core/arrays/integer.py", line 65, in _safe_cast
    casted = values.astype(dtype, copy=copy)
OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long
```

`lib.infer_dtype` reports `"integer"` for these values, and the object-block conversion maps
that straight to `Int64` without checking that the values actually fit. `IntegerArray._safe_cast`
first attempts `astype(..., casting="safe")`, which raises `TypeError` for object input, and the
fallback `values.astype(dtype)` is what raises `OverflowError`.

Note this is a plain `OverflowError` escaping a public API rather than a pandas error type, so
it is also not catchable via anything in `pandas.errors`.

### Expected Behavior

`convert_dtypes` should leave the column as `object` when the values do not fit in the target
integer dtype, matching what construction already infers:

```python
>>> pd.Series([2**64], dtype=object).convert_dtypes().dtype
dtype('O')
```

Raising a clear pandas-level error would also be defensible, but silently attempting `Int64` and
surfacing a raw `OverflowError` is not.

### Issue Description

`times` that are equally spaced should be equivalent to not passing `times` at all —
that invariant is asserted directly by `test_ewma_with_times_equal_spacing`. It holds
for three of the four `adjust` × `ignore_na` combinations, but breaks for
`adjust=False, ignore_na=False` once the data contains `NaN`:

```python
data = np.arange(10.0)
data[::2] = np.nan
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": data})
times = pd.date_range("2000", freq="D", periods=10)

for adjust in (True, False):
    for ignore_na in (True, False):
        lhs = df.ewm(halflife="1D", times=times, adjust=adjust, ignore_na=ignore_na).mean()
        rhs = df.ewm(halflife=1.0, adjust=adjust, ignore_na=ignore_na).mean()
        print(adjust, ignore_na, np.allclose(lhs, rhs, equal_nan=True))

# True  True   True
# True  False  True
# False True   True
# False False  False   <-- diverges
```

The two paths generalize `adjust=False` to a gap of `Δ` differently. They agree at
`Δ = 1` and diverge otherwise:

- no `times` — normalized, matching the recursion documented for `ignore_na`:
  `y_t = ((1-α)^Δ · y_u + α · x_t) / ((1-α)^Δ + α)`
- `times` — convex, added in GH-59142 to support irregular intervals:
  `y_t = (1-α)^Δ · y_u + (1 - (1-α)^Δ) · x_t`

With `ignore_na=False` a `NaN` gap pushes `Δ` above 1, so the two disagree.

`test_ewma_with_times_equal_spacing` does not catch this because it is not
parametrized over `adjust`, and GH-59142's own `test_ewma_with_times_variable_spacing`
uses `np.arange(3)` with no `NaN`, so the interaction with `NaN` was never covered.

Worth noting: this divergence is *newly visible* as of GH-66521. Before that fix both
spellings agreed — but they agreed on the wrong value, because the `com == 1` special
case intended for the `times` path was leaking into the no-`times` path (GH-31178).
GH-66521 deliberately fixed only the no-`times` path and left `times` exactly as 3.0
shipped it, which is what surfaces the inconsistency.

### Expected Behavior

Undecided, and that is really the question here — the two candidate generalizations
are both defensible, so this needs a call on intended semantics:

1. **Make `times` normalized across `NaN` gaps**, restoring the equal-spacing
   invariant and making GH-31178's example return `3.666667` in both spellings. Note
   this cannot be done by simply switching the `times` path to the normalized form:
   `test_ewma_with_times_variable_spacing` value-pins the convex form for
   `adjust=False` (`0.2376251864...`; the normalized form gives `0.39608`). It would
   require distinguishing decay from elapsed interval from decay accumulated across
   skipped `NaN` rows.
2. **Declare the convex form correct for `times`** and document that
   `ignore_na=False` weights `NaN` gaps differently once `times` is supplied,
   accepting that equally spaced `times` is not equivalent to no `times` in this one
   combination.

  That's not a major difficulty but it means that implementing callback support is tied to metadata-routing if you want full capacity (it might be possible to make it optional and then callbacks would be limited when there's no metadata-routing, as it's the case now)

  LogisticRegression is not a consumer of ``amount``: it has no idea which one is for which set. In fact amount_train is not even useful here so I could have just passed amount=amount_val.

Follow-ups found while fixing GH-66510 for the vectorized offset paths. Each is pre-existing on
`main` (verified at `082e7739`) and out of scope for that PR, but they are the same family of bug:
arithmetic on the raw int64 datetime64 values either lands on the `NaT` sentinel or leaves the
representable range without being reported as such.

Filing as one issue because (1) and (2) each need their two halves fixed together, and the whole
set shares a root cause. Happy to split if that's easier to triage.

### 1. Adding a timedelta can silently produce `NaT`

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so a result that lands exactly there is indistinguishable from `NaT`
downstream. `add_overflowsafe` checks for int64 overflow but not for this, and the scalar
`_Timestamp.__add__` does not check either:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.min + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
NaT
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.min]) + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.TimedeltaIndex([pd.Timedelta.min]) - pd.Timedelta(1, "ns")
TimedeltaIndex(['NaT'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.PeriodIndex([pd.Period(ordinal=-2**63 + 1, freq="D")]) - 1
PeriodIndex(['NaT'], dtype='period[D]')
```

All four should raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. Both the scalar and the
array side need to change together — fixing only one would replace this with a scalar/array
disagreement.

### 2. Out-of-bounds month and quarter shifts raise `OverflowError` from the vendored C

`shift_months`, `shift_quarters` and `SemiMonthOffset._apply_array` build their results with
`npy_datetimestruct_to_datetime`, whose overflow check surfaces as a bare `OverflowError` naming
a C source line, where the scalar path raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`:

```python
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../pandas/_libs/src/vendored/numpy/datetime/np_datetime.c:512
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
OutOfBoundsDatetime: Cannot cast 2262-05-11 23:47:16.854775 to unit='ns' without overflow.
```

Same for `MonthEnd`, `QuarterEnd`, `SemiMonthEnd`, `YearEnd`.

Relatedly, because the month shift is materialized before the timedelta component is applied, a
composed offset whose *final* result is representable is rejected on the array path:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
Timestamp('2262-04-10 23:47:16.854775807')
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../np_datetime.c:512
```

Fixing that means applying the two components in one pass so the out-of-range intermediate is
never stored.

### 3. `SemiMonthOffset` and `shift_quarters` truncate `n` to 32 bits

`n` is held in a C `int`, so a multiple of `2**32` silently becomes a no-op:

```python
>>> dr = pd.date_range("2000-01-03", periods=1, unit="s")
>>> dr + pd.offsets.SemiMonthEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-15'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == SemiMonthEnd(0)
>>> dr + pd.offsets.QuarterEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-03-31'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == QuarterEnd(0)
```

`BusinessDay` and `Week` had the same bug; widening those to `int64_t` is what the GH-66510
follow-up PR does, and the same treatment applies here.

### 4. `ccalendar` truncates years above `2**31`

`dayofweek(int y, int m, int d)`, `year_add_months` and `month_add_months` take the year as a C
`int`, but `npy_datetimestruct.year` is `int64_t`. Reachable only at second resolution, where the
representable range runs to year ~2.9e11:

```python
>>> big = pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.iinfo(np.int64).max], dtype="M8[s]"))
>>> big[0]
Timestamp('292277026596-12-04 15:30:07')
>>> big + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
DatetimeIndex(['219250469-01-04 15:30:07'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # wrapped
>>> big[0].weekday()
OverflowError: value too large to convert to int
```

The weekday truncation also silently gives `BusinessDay` the wrong anchor for such dates, rather
than raising.

### 5. Minor: duplicated `checked_*` externs

`portable.h`'s `checked_add` / `checked_sub` / `checked_mul` are declared in a `cdef extern` block
in `tzconversion.pyx` and again in `offsets.pyx`, with different signatures (`int` vs `bint`, with
and without `noexcept nogil`). Worth hoisting into a shared `.pxd` so they cannot drift.

Identical source, identical runner. Note the attribution: `run_repro.py:10`
is `df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()` — the *caller*, which performs no
assignment at all. In a larger application this misattribution points at

the application's `MainLoop()` call in the entry module), which makes the
warning extremely hard to trace back to its real origin.

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.__setitem__` (pandas 3.0.3, `pandas/core/frame.py:4642`; the same
pattern guards every `ChainedAssignmentError` site in `frame.py`,
`series.py`, `generic.py`, and `indexing.py`) detects chained assignment
with two heuristics:

```python
if not CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED:
    if sys.getrefcount(self) <= REF_COUNT and not com.is_local_in_caller_frame(self):
        warnings.warn(_chained_assignment_msg, ChainedAssignmentError, stacklevel=2)
```

Both heuristics assume the caller is interpreted CPython code, and both
misfire when the caller is a compiled extension:

1. **Refcount** — a Cython function keeps `df` in a C variable rather than
   in a frame's locals, so `sys.getrefcount(df)` inside `__setitem__` sits
   at the temporary-object level even though `df` is a genuine local.
2. **Frame inspection** — `is_local_in_caller_frame`
   (`pandas/core/common.py:662`) looks for the object in
   `sys._getframe(2).f_locals`. Cython functions do not create Python frame
   objects, so `sys._getframe(2)` skips past the real caller entirely and
   lands on an unrelated pure-Python frame further down the stack. The
   rescue check fails, and `stacklevel=2` attributes the warning to that
   unrelated frame.

The same failure mode applies to any frame-less caller (Cython, mypyc, and
similar ahead-of-time compilers).

Filtering the warning is not a real workaround: with
`warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=ChainedAssignmentError)` the
message disappears but the detection machinery still runs. Because the
refcount test always passes for compiled callers, **every** setitem from
compiled code takes the slow path — `sys._getframe(2)`, a full `f_locals`
materialisation, and the `warnings` machinery. We measured roughly 4 µs per
assignment on small frames (Python 3.11, Windows) — a permanent tax on
exactly the code that was compiled for speed.

A short-circuit for this already exists: `CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED`
(`pandas/compat/_constants.py`) skips the whole block, including both
heuristics. But it is a constant computed from the interpreter type
(`= PYPY`) — informational only, with no supported way for an application
to set it.

Suggested fix — either or both:

- Provide a supported opt-out that feeds `CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED`, e.g.
  an environment variable (`PANDAS_CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED=1`), mirroring
  how `PANDAS_COPY_ON_WRITE` was handled during the CoW rollout.
- Suppress the warning when frame inspection cannot positively identify the
  caller (i.e. when the frame walk cannot see the object at all): a
  heuristic that cannot observe its evidence should not fire.

### Expected Behavior

A plain `df["b"] = ...` on a function-local DataFrame should not raise
`ChainedAssignmentError` regardless of whether the enclosing function is
interpreted or compiled — and applications embedding pandas in compiled
code should have a supported way to opt out of the detection overhead
entirely.

### Issue Description

`Parser.process_byte_array_with_data` takes its bounds as C `int`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/_libs/sas.pyx#L541

```cython
cdef void process_byte_array_with_data(self, int offset, int length) except *:
    ...
    assert offset + length <= self.cached_page_len, "Out of bounds read"
    source = Buffer(&self.cached_page[offset], length)
```

`length` is `row_length`, read straight from the file as an unsigned int. When it is near `INT_MAX`, `offset + length` overflows signed `int` and wraps negative, so the guard passes. `Buffer` is then constructed with a ~2GB `length` over a 64KB page. `buf_get`'s own `assert offset < buf.length` is satisfied for reads far past the real allocation, so every subsequent read is unchecked and the process dies on a wild address.

A more modest `row_length` (e.g. `0x20000000`) is caught cleanly by the assert — it is specifically the overflow that defeats it. Widening these parameters to `int64_t`/`Py_ssize_t` and validating `row_length` against the page size after parsing the row-size subheader would fix it.

This is **not** fixed by #66469, which validates
`offsets[j] + lengths[j] <= row_length` once in `Parser.__init__`. That check passes
trivially here — the column offsets and lengths are untouched, it is `row_length` itself
that is out of range — so the crash above reproduces with #66469 applied.

Two related unchecked accesses in the same loop, noted for completeness:

1. The 8-byte fast path added in #65363 reads without a bounds check, unlike the `else`
   branch it replaced, which used the checked `buf_get`. **Already fixed by #66469**;
   mentioned here only because it shares this function and I hit it while narrowing down
   the crash.

2. The function is `@cython.boundscheck(False)` / `@cython.wraparound(False)`, and the
   destination index `m = s + 8 - lngt` goes negative for a decimal column declaring
   `lngt > 8`. Nothing validates `3 <= lngt <= 8`, and #66469's check does not catch it
   either (a column can declare `lngt > 8` while still fitting inside the row). Patching
   column 0 of `test1.sas7bdat` to declare length 16 does not crash, but writes 8 bytes
   in front of `byte_chunk` and returns a silently wrong frame.

`row_count`, `column_count`, and the subheader offset/length pairs are also file-controlled
and reach this arithmetic; a too-large `column_count` is caught, but only incidentally, by
an `IndexError` in `_parse_metadata`.

### Expected Behavior

A malformed or truncated SAS7BDAT should raise, not segfault. `test_corrupt_read` already covers a truncated file, so the intent is there — it just does not extend to metadata whose values are internally inconsistent.

This matters beyond developer error: `.sas7bdat` files are routinely received from third parties, so the parser is effectively parsing untrusted input.
